newsitem.title: FRANCE: "No surrender" by Algeria's GIA deputy - papers.
newsitem.headline: "No surrender" by Algeria's GIA deputy - papers.

text.p: Algerian newspapers, in reports that appeared on Wednesday to have been inspired by the authorities, dismissed as untrue the reported surrender of a leader of the feared Armed Islamic Group (GIA).
Algeria's official news agency APS carried a roundup of the newspaper reports which denied that the GIA number two Radouane Makador had surrendered last month.
According to APS, the newspaper said the original report of him giving himself up was "prelude to a new internal war...between the emirs" of the GIA.
Liberte newspaper, a day after reporting the surrender, said in fact Makador had been wounded in a clash in the Chrea hills south of Algiers nearly a month ago but had succeeded in escaping.
On Tuesday, Liberte carried an apparent statement from the GIA condemning Makador as a traitor and saying he had given information on the GIA leadership, structure and bases to the security forces.
The statement ordered GIA activists in Algeria and abroad to cut links with him.
Algerian newspapers on Wednesday quoted "sure" and "credible" sources to dismiss the report, said APS.
Liberte said the communique aimed only a "masking a mini coup d'etat aiming at the pure and simple liquidation of Redouane Makador by a rival faction within the GIA."
The evening newspaper Horizon said Makador, known for "his terrorism and barbarity" had not surrendered and that it was not the first time the GIA had been subject to a similar "purge".

The GIA is blamed by the authorities for most of the savage killings in Algeria, including massacres of villagers, the murder of journalists, intellectuals and foreigners, and the kidnapping and raping of girls.

The Algerian government, fighting a an armed Moslem rebel campaign, last May offered residents up to 4.5 million dinars ($80,357) for information leading to the capture or killing of the country's most wanted guerrillas.
Among those sought by the authorities were Radouane and the GIA's leader Antar Zouabri.

About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists took a commanding lead. New elections were held last month in which moderate Islamists were allowed to compete.
